title: Count Hills and Valleys in an Array
statement: For an index `i` of the integer array `nums`, look left for the nearest index whose value differs from `nums[i]`, and look right in the same way. If both exist and both values are smaller than `nums[i]`, index `i` belongs to a **hill**; if both exist and both are larger, it belongs to a **valley**. An index with no differing value on one of its sides is in neither. A maximal block of adjacent equal values forms a single hill or valley, however long it is. Return the total number of hills and valleys in `nums`.
notes:
## Intuition

A block of equal values is one hill or one valley, so it is enough to judge each block once, at its last index, where the right neighbour is guaranteed to differ. The left side needs only one remembered number: the value of the previous block, which is the nearest different value to the left. The literal approach (scan outwards from every index for its nearest different neighbours) also works for 100 values; the single pass simply avoids the repeated scanning.

## Approach

1. Set `count = 0` and `left = nums[0]`, the value of the block before the current one.
2. Walk `i` from 1 to `nums.length - 2` (the first and last index never qualify).
3. If `nums[i]` equals `nums[i + 1]`, the block continues; skip to the next index.
4. Otherwise `i` ends its block. It is a hill if it is above both `left` and `nums[i + 1]`, a valley if it is below both. Count it if either holds.
5. Set `left = nums[i]`: this block is now the previous one.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2,4,1,1,6,5]`, `left = 2`.

- `i = 1`: 4 is above `left = 2` and above 1: a hill, `count = 1`, `left = 4`.
- `i = 2`: `nums[3]` is also 1, so skip.
- `i = 3`: 1 is below `left = 4` and below 6: a valley, `count = 2`, `left = 1`.
- `i = 4`: 6 is above 1 and above 5: a hill, `count = 3`.

The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is looked at once.
- Space: O(1): only `count` and `left` are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Counting every index of a flat block separately: `[2,1,1,2]` has one valley, not two.
- Comparing with `nums[i - 1]` instead of the nearest different value fails inside flat stretches.
- A block that touches either end of the array has no differing neighbour on that side, so it never counts; starting `left` at `nums[0]` handles a leading block automatically.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | hills and valleys found so far |
| `left` | value of the previous block (nearest different value to the left) |
| `i` | current index |
| `isHill`, `isValley` | whether the block ending at `i` is a hill or a valley |

narration.2: No hills or valleys have been found yet.
narration.3: left remembers the value of the previous block; it starts as the first value.
narration.5: The first and last index can never be hills or valleys, so look only at the ones between.
narration.6: The next value is the same, so this block is not finished yet.
narration.7: Skip: the block will be judged once, at its last index.
narration.9: A hill rises above both its left block and the value right after it.
narration.10: A valley sits below both of them.
narration.14: This block becomes the nearest different value for the next block.
narration.16: Every block has been judged; return the total.
